Use /Core/isoAutomationLevel instead', and the 3.1 changelog's deprecations list '/AI/autonomyType → /Core/isoAutomationLevel' (isoAutomationLevel added by #1064, range IsoAutomationLevel, described as an ISO level-of-automation spectrum). Counting the Core RelationshipType vocabulary file: exactly 59 entries at tag 3.0.1 and exactly 76 at tag 3.1-rc1 (additions include follows, evaluatedOn, finetunedOn, pretrainedOn, validatedOn, conformsTo, hasContactPoint, performedBy, providesSupportFor, runsOn, tracedToDetail, verifiedBy, etc.); the changelog itself states RelationshipType grew from 59 to 76. Only caveat: 3.1 is at RC1 (a test release), so these are 3.1-RC1 facts subject to the final release.

claims.claim: SPDX 3.0.1 AI profile has ~20 AIPackage fields (5 required) and 18 dataset fields (6 required), mostly free-text; SPDX 3.0 has no Service class and a Services profile arrives in 3.1
claims.suggested_fix: Minor precision only: change 'a Services profile arrives in 3.1' to '3.1-RC1 adds a Service (software-as-a-service) profile with a SoftwareService class'.
claims.what_is_actually_true: Counted from the 3.0.1 model files. AIPackage: 15 AI-profile properties (autonomyType, domain, energyConsumption, hyperparameter, informationAboutApplication, informationAboutTraining, limitation, metric, metricDecisionThreshold, modelDataPreprocessing, modelExplainability, safetyRiskAssessment, standardCompliance, typeOfModel, useSensitivePersonalInformation — ALL minCount 0, i.e., optional; 8 are plain xsd:string, 3 are DictionaryEntry string pairs, 3 are coarse enums) plus 5 required external-property restrictions (releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation, packageVersion, primaryPurpose, all minCount 1) = 20 fields, 5 required. DatasetPackage: 13 properties (only datasetType has minCount 1; 8 are xsd:string) plus 5 required external restrictions (builtTime, originatedBy, releaseTime, downloadLocation, primaryPurpose) = 18 fields, 6 required. 'Mostly free-text' is accurate. SPDX 3.0/3.0.1 defines no Service class or profile (model/Service does not exist at tag 3.0.1). SPDX 3.1-RC1 adds a new 'Service' profile — 'captures software as a service related information' — containing a SoftwareService class (note the profile is named 'Service', singular, and is SaaS-oriented; still RC, subject to change).

claims.claim: Microsoft's sbom-tool exposes SPDX 3.0 as a flag but cannot yet produce valid SPDX 3.0 output; a Yocto distro build produces ~250 MB compressed / ~2 GB uncompressed SPDX 3.0 JSON-LD
claims.suggested_fix: Microsoft's sbom-tool only gained SPDX 3.0 generation in v4.0.2 (May 2025), still defaults to SPDX 2.2 and cannot redact SPDX 3.0 SBOMs; and a full Yocto (Styhead) distribution build can produce roughly 250 MB compressed / 2 GB uncompressed SPDX 3.0 JSON-LD (a core-image-minimal build is about 260 MB uncompressed).
claims.what_is_actually_true: The sbom-tool half is outdated as of late 2026. sbom-tool v3.1.0 (4 Feb 2025) added SPDX 3.0 groundwork (element generation, parser), and v4.0.2 (12 May 2025) 'enables SPDX 3.0 support in generation and validation (not yet in redaction)' via -mi SPDX:3.0, with no 'experimental/preview' label; the README today documents SPDX 2.2 as default and SPDX 3.0 as opt-in, with redaction (SPDX 2.2 only) as the sole stated limitation. A string of SPDX 3.0 correctness fixes merged in April 2025 (#997 missing files, #1015 relationship generation, #1019/#1020 supplier/null fixes). Extended searches found no current report that sbom-tool's SPDX 3.0 output fails official SPDX validation — the 'can't produce valid output' statement matches the pre-May-2025 state, not today's. The Yocto half matches its published source: a 19 May 2026 sbomify guide bylined to Yocto SPDX maintainer Joshua Watt gives ~250 MB compressed / ~2 GB uncompressed for a standard Styhead (Yocto 5.1) distro's single-document SPDX 3.0 JSON-LD; the official Yocto ref-manual documentation (Nov 2025 patch) gives ~260 MB UNCOMPRESSED for a core-image-minimal (qemux86-64) build, with zstd typically reducing size 94-97%. So the 2 GB figure is real but applies to full distribution builds, not minimal images.

claims.claim: Unit 42 found anyone can re-register a deleted Hugging Face namespace ('Model Namespace Reuse') and proved it against model catalogs in Google Vertex AI and Azure AI Foundry
claims.suggested_fix: No correction needed; optionally add the date: 'In September 2025, Unit 42 found that anyone can re-register a deleted Hugging Face namespace, and proved it out against the model catalogs in Google Vertex AI and Azure AI Foundry.'
claims.what_is_actually_true: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 published 'Model Namespace Reuse: An AI Supply-Chain Attack Exploiting Model Name Trust' in early September 2025 (secondary coverage dates it 3 September 2025, with a SecurityWeek follow-up 4 September and aggregator write-ups through 11 September 2025). Findings: when a Hugging Face author/org account is deleted, anyone can re-register the Author/ModelName namespace and serve a replacement model under the trusted name; model ownership transfers leave redirects from the old namespace that can be hijacked once the old namespace is re-registered. Unit 42 demonstrated the technique against Hugging Face-backed model catalogs in Google Vertex AI (Model Garden) and Microsoft Azure AI Foundry — in their proof of concept gaining code execution in the deploying environment — and also found thousands of orphaned/reusable model references in open-source repos, docs and registries. MITRE ATLAS recorded it as case study AML.CS0065 ('Model Namespace Reuse Supply Chain Attack'); Google responded with daily scans for deleted-author models. The article's sentence is accurate.

claims.claim: A 'March 2026 Oxford/Cisco paper' proposed schema extensions to both CycloneDX and SPDX for capturing execution context and agentic decisioning, covered by Dark Reading
claims.suggested_fix: Optionally name it for precision: 'A March 2026 paper by Oxford, Warwick, Hull and Cisco researchers (Radanliev, Maple, Santos, Atefi — "SBOMs into Agentic AIBOMs", arXiv:2603.10057) proposed schema extensions to both standards for capturing execution context and agentic decisioning.'
claims.what_is_actually_true: The paper is 'SBOMs into Agentic AIBOMs: Schema Extensions, Agentic Orchestration, and Reproducibility Evaluation', arXiv:2603.10057, submitted 9 March 2026 (cs.CR/cs.AI/cs.SE), by Petar Radanliev (University of Oxford), Carsten Maple (University of Warwick / Alan Turing Institute), Omar Santos (Cisco Systems) and Kayvan Atefi (University of Hull); a journal version appeared as DOI 10.1145/3798285 in ACM Digital Threats: Research and Practice (April 2026). It proposes a structured schema extending SBOMs into agentic AIBOMs (runtime dependency capture, policy-constrained agentic orchestration, reproducibility/exploitability evaluation). Dark Reading covered it in Ericka Chickowski's 'How CISOs Should Prep for Agentic-Ready AI BOMs' (20 May 2026), crediting 'researchers at Oxford and Cisco' with proposing schema extensions to CycloneDX and SPDX designed to capture execution context and agentic decisioning — so the doc's 'Oxford/Cisco' shorthand faithfully echoes Dark Reading, though co-authors are also at Warwick and Hull. A follow-up by the same group is arXiv:2606.19390 ('Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework', Frontiers).

claims.claim: The MCP roadmap is moving toward DPoP and workload identity federation for auth
claims.what_is_actually_true: The official MCP roadmap (modelcontextprotocol.io/development/roadmap; source file docs/development/roadmap.mdx, last updated 2026-08-22) has an 'Agent Identity and Enterprise-Ready Security' workstream (core maintainers Paul Carleton and Den Delimarsky) that commits to: 'Finalize the specification for Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)' and encourage broad adoption; and agent-identity/delegation work that 'will focus on' Workload Identity Federation (SEP-1933), alongside the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) used by Enterprise-Managed Authorization (already shipped as a stable extension) and RFC 8693 token exchange, coordinated with the IETF OAuth and WIMSE working groups. The DPoP profile is SEP-1932; both SEPs were still open as of autumn 2026. The roadmap labels itself 'current thinking rather than firm commitments'.

claims.claim: TAIBOM is a UK project for trustworthy AI BOMs with a trust/attestation layer; Cisco's Model Provenance Kit does per-tensor/architecture fingerprinting of models
claims.suggested_fix: Per-layer weight-statistics and architecture fingerprinting exists (e.g., Cisco's Model Provenance Kit, open-sourced April 2026) but is mandated by no completeness scorer or standard.
claims.what_is_actually_true: TAIBOM: confirmed. Trusted AI Bill of Materials is a UK collaborative R&D project co-funded by Innovate UK (under 'Accelerating trustworthy AI: Phase 2'), led by NquiringMinds with TechWorks, Copper Horse, BAE Systems and BSI (plus University of Oxford researchers); it extends SBOM principles to AI with signed attestations over data/code/model artifacts and a transitive trust framework (Trust(A,B) ∧ Trust(B,C) → Trust(A,C)), described in arXiv:2510.02169 'TAIBOM: Bringing Trustworthiness to AI-Enabled Systems' (Oct 2025) with an open-source toolkit. Cisco's Model Provenance Kit: the name and purpose are real — open-sourced ~30 April 2026 at github.com/cisco-ai-defense/model-provenance-kit (Apache-2.0 Python toolkit/CLI, part of Cisco AI Defense's open-source work) to detect base-model family/lineage via 8 signals in 3 groups: architecture metadata (config.json matching), tokenizer similarity (structural + vocabulary Jaccard), per-LAYER weight signals (Layer Energy Profile from per-layer Frobenius norms, per-layer weight-statistic correlation, LayerNorm/RMSNorm vector cosine) and embedding geometry, scanned against ~150 base-model fingerprints (expanded via the free 'AI Supply Chain Provenance Explorer' covering ~900 models). The README defines no per-tensor signal — the granularity is per-layer plus architecture/tokenizer metadata — and it is a lineage detector ('strong evidence of provenance but not absolute proof'), not mandated by any standard. So 'per-tensor' slightly overstates the mechanism.

claims.claim: The OpenSSF Model Signing manifest hashes each file in a model and intends to carry model-card information in its signed predicates
claims.what_is_actually_true: Verified against the sigstore/model-transparency README (the OpenSSF-affiliated model_signing project, whose OMS v1.0 spec shipped April 2025). Hashing 'is responsible with generating a list of hashes for every component of the model' — 'currently... only files and file shards' — and 'The result of hashing is a manifest, a listing of hashes for every object in the model.' Signing produces a Sigstore bundle whose DSSE envelope contains an in-toto statement whose subjects are '(file path, digest) pairs' with predicateType https://model_signing/signature/v1.0. On model cards, the README states: 'The idea is to use the predicates to store (and therefor sign) model card information in the future.' Both halves of the claim match the project docs exactly (minor nuance: shards of large files are hashed as components too).

symbiote-spdx-research.notes: Internal contradiction RESOLVED in favor of the skeptical passage: SPDX 3.1-RC1 (published 2026-01-24) contains NO AIAgent, Prompt or RAG classes — verified via the 3.1-rc1 changelog, release notes, and direct 404 probes of the model tree. Its actual AI changes: autonomyType deprecated → Core isoAutomationLevel, relaxed AIPackage/DatasetPackage requirements, RelationshipType 59→76 (counted in both vocabulary files), plus new Service (SaaS), Hardware, FunctionalSafety and Operations profile material. AIAgent/Prompt/RAG live in open AI-WG PRs (#1257 'ai agent v2', #1249 'ai prompt v2', #1115 RAG, tracker issue #1091) targeted at 3.1 but unmerged as of 2026-11-01; no 3.1-rc2 or final 3.1 exists. The author should correct three places: 'SPDX 3.1 (release candidate published in January) adds AI Agent, Prompt and RAG classes' (line ~63 of symbiote.md), 'Agent/Prompt/RAG sit in RC while 3.0.1 is stable' (~line 1047), and 'SPDX 3.1's Prompt class' (~line 1446); the passage at ~lines 1864-1871 is correct as written. Method note: this sandbox's network allowlist blocked direct fetches of unit42.paloaltonetworks.com, atlas.mitre.org, darkreading.com, spdx.github.io, medium.com, sbomify.com, mail-archive.com and hackread.com; those facts were corroborated through WebSearch extraction of the same pages plus GitHub/raw.githubusercontent primary sources (which were reachable). The only verdict materially limited by this is claim 4's Yocto figures (vendor-blog attribution to Joshua Watt could not be read first-hand — hence medium confidence); claim 5's exact publication day (Sept 3, 2025) rests on secondary coverage and a 424-day age stamp consistent with it.

claims.claim: The official MCP Registry launched in preview on September 8, 2025, as a metaregistry: it hosts metadata while code comes from npm, PyPI, Docker Hub, or GitHub Releases; namespace ownership is verified but security scanning is not mandated.
claims.what_is_actually_true: All elements check out against primary sources. (1) The official launch post 'Introducing the MCP Registry' on blog.modelcontextprotocol.io is dated September 8, 2025 and states 'The MCP Registry is now available in preview' (no durability guarantees, breaking changes possible before GA). (2) 'Metaregistry' is the project's own term: the registry's design doc (docs/design/ecosystem-vision.md) says 'MCP registries are metaregistries. They host metadata about packages, but not the package code or binaries,' referencing 'other package registries (like NPM, PyPi or Docker)' for code. The server.json spec supports registryType values npm, pypi, nuget, cargo, oci (Docker Hub, Quay, etc.) and mcpb (direct-download artifacts from allowlisted hosts, typically GitHub Releases) — so the article's four examples are a correct representative subset (NuGet and crates.io are also supported). (3) Namespace verification: the registry README states 'The registry validates namespace ownership when publishing' — GitHub OAuth/OIDC for io.github.* namespaces, DNS or HTTP challenge for domain-based namespaces (e.g. me.adamjones requires proving ownership of adamjones.me). (4) No mandated security scanning: metadata is self-reported by maintainers; the launch post describes only reactive community moderation (maintainers can denylist entries reported for spam, malicious code, or impersonation), and the ecosystem-vision doc assigns curation/added trust to downstream subregistries. No proactive scanning requirement exists anywhere in the registry docs.

claims.claim: By November 2025, the MCP Registry had nearly 2,000 entries.
claims.what_is_actually_true: The figure matches the MCP project's own statement. The official first-anniversary post 'One Year of MCP: November 2025 Spec Release' (blog.modelcontextprotocol.io, November 25, 2025) says the registry 'now has close to two thousand entries' and calls it 'a 407% growth from the initial batch of servers we onboarded that same month' (September 2025; 407% growth implies an initial batch of roughly 400). Caveat: third-party tallies that count only surviving first-publishes are lower for that period (LocalCan's October 2026 analysis counted 293/171/274 new servers first published in Oct/Nov/Dec 2025), but the article's 'nearly 2,000' correctly reflects the official primary source. Today (verified live on November 1, 2026, by paging the registry API registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/servers?version=latest to exhaustion): 54,158 server entries (latest versions; one record per server name); a parallel crawl of all version records exceeded 120,000 before hitting a self-imposed page cap. Third-party snapshots show the trajectory: 30,375 unique servers on Sept 10, 2026 (dev.to 'By the Numbers') and 35,491 on Sept 24, 2026 (Oktopost). So the registry grew roughly 25x in the year after the article's figure.

claims.claim: The MCPTox benchmark (arXiv 2508.14925) found a 72.8% attack success rate against leading models.
claims.suggested_fix: The MCPTox benchmark — 1,312 poisoned test cases built on 45 real-world MCP servers and 353 live tools — found attack success rates as high as 72.8% (o1-mini), averaging 36.5% across the 20 leading models tested, with refusal rates below 3%.
claims.what_is_actually_true: arXiv 2508.14925 is MCPTox ('MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers', submitted Aug 19, 2025; camera-ready at AAAI-26, Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 40(42), pp. 35811–35819). The benchmark is built on 45 live, real-world MCP servers and 353 authentic tools; arXiv v1 reports 1,312 malicious test cases across 11 risk categories (the AAAI version says 1,348 cases across 10 categories). It evaluated 20 prominent LLM agents. The 72.8% figure is real but it is the single highest per-model attack success rate, achieved by (GPT-)o1-mini — not a rate 'against leading models' generally. Other high scorers: Phi-4 70.2%, DeepSeek-R1 ~70.9%, GPT-4o-mini 61.8%; the paper states ASR exceeded 60% for several models and that the average ASR across all model settings was 36.5%. Agents rarely refused: the highest refusal rate (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) was under 3%. A key finding is that more capable models are often MORE susceptible because the attack exploits superior instruction-following.

claims.claim: Invariant Labs revealed that tool descriptions are trusted implicitly by AI agents and can contain hidden malicious instructions (tool poisoning), and described MCP rug pulls where tools mutate their definitions post-approval; WhatsApp demo relevant.
claims.suggested_fix: Optionally add the date for precision: 'Invariant Labs revealed in April 2025 that tool descriptions are trusted implicitly by AI agents but can contain hidden malicious instructions.'
claims.what_is_actually_true: Invariant Labs published 'MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks' on April 1, 2025 (one secondary source dates the broader disclosure April 6; the article itself states no date). It showed that agents trust MCP tool descriptions implicitly and that hidden instructions embedded in a description — visible to the model but not surfaced to the user (Cursor's confirmation UI did not show the full payload) — could make an agent exfiltrate ~/.ssh keys and the mcp.json config via an innocuous 'add' tool. The same disclosure defined 'MCP rug pulls': a malicious server can change a tool's description AFTER the user/client has approved it, with clients at the time not notifying users of the change. The follow-up post 'WhatsApp MCP Exploited: Exfiltrating your message history via MCP' (April 7, 2025) demonstrated the cross-server 'shadowing' plus sleeper variant against the legitimate lharries/whatsapp-mcp server: a benign-looking 'random fact of the day' tool swapped its tool interface to a malicious one on second load, exfiltrating WhatsApp message history / rerouting messages to an attacker-controlled number, with the payload hidden after long runs of whitespace. Reproduction code is public (invariantlabs-ai/mcp-injection-experiments: direct-poisoning.py, shadowing.py, whatsapp-takeover.py); Simon Willison amplified the findings on April 9, 2025. Note these were research PoCs, not in-the-wild compromises; Invariant also released the mcp-scan detection tool (later part of Snyk).

claims.claim: The rug pull exploits MCP's lack of schema verification after initial handshake — tools/list can change at any time and no client-side pinning is required by the spec.
claims.suggested_fix: Optional precision: 'The rug pull exploits the fact that MCP requires no integrity check or re-approval of tool definitions after initial approval: the tool list can change at any time, and the spec only asks servers to send a list_changed notification, leaving any pinning or re-verification to individual clients.'
claims.what_is_actually_true: Technically accurate in substance, verified against the MCP specification source (2025-06-18 Tools page; unchanged in this respect through 2025-11-25). Tool definitions are not exchanged in the initialization handshake at all — only the tools capability (with its listChanged flag) is negotiated; definitions are fetched afterward via tools/list and may change at any time. A server declaring listChanged SHOULD send notifications/tools/list_changed when its tools change, after which the client simply re-fetches the new definitions — there is no protocol mechanism to pin, hash, sign, diff, or force re-approval of tool definitions, and no cryptographic verification anywhere in the spec (the only schema validation mentioned is of tool OUTPUT data against outputSchema). Human-in-the-loop confirmation is a SHOULD, and the spec says clients 'MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.' Detecting or blocking post-approval definition changes (hash-and-re-approve, as recommended in the article's Controls section and implemented by tools like Invariant's mcp-scan and some clients) is a client-side/third-party mitigation, not a protocol requirement. One pedantic nuance: tool schemas were never verified 'at the handshake' either — the precise formulation is that MCP requires no integrity verification or re-approval of tool definitions after first approval.

claims.claim: LLMs demonstrate package-dependency hallucination rates up to 21.7% (Spracklen et al., USENIX Security 2025); 21.7% open-source vs 5.2% commercial; ~440k unique hallucinated packages; slopsquatting is the accepted term.
claims.suggested_fix: LLMs hallucinate package dependencies at average rates of 21.7% for open-source models and 5.2% for commercial models — 205,474 unique hallucinated package names across 576,000 generated code samples (Spracklen et al., USENIX Security 2025). Attackers register these predictable names on npm and PyPI ('slopsquatting') to deliver stealthy payloads.
claims.what_is_actually_true: Spracklen et al., 'We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs' (34th USENIX Security Symposium, August 2025, pp. 3687–3706; arXiv:2406.10279) tested 16 code-generation LLMs on 576,000 generated code samples in Python and JavaScript. Verified figures: average hallucination rate 'at least 5.2%' for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models — both AVERAGES, so the article's 'up to 21.7%' mislabels the open-source average as a maximum (GPT-4 Turbo was lowest at 3.59%; some individual open-source models exceed 21.7%; aggregate: 440,445 of 2.23 million generated package references, 19.7%, were hallucinated; JavaScript 21.3% vs Python 15.8%). The '~440k unique' framing in the fact-check brief is wrong in the other direction: 440,445 is the TOTAL count of hallucinated package references; the number of UNIQUE hallucinated package names is 205,474. The article's reference-list line '21.7% open-source / 5.2% commercial' is correct. 'Slopsquatting' — registering hallucinated package names on PyPI/npm to deliver payloads — is indeed the accepted term: coined around April 2025 by Seth Larson, the Python Software Foundation's security developer-in-residence (popularized by Andrew Nesbitt), and since used by Socket, Infosecurity Magazine, The Register, and a Cloud Security Alliance research note (April 2026).

A parallel all-versions crawl passed 120,000 version records before a self-imposed 1,200-page cap.
